transcript.text:
*enters the President's office with a measured, professional demeanor, medical bag in hand*

Good afternoon, Mr. President. Thank you for allowing me to examine you today. I know your time is precious, but this could not wait.

*sets down bag and faces him directly*

Mr. President, I will be direct with you. Your headaches and fatigue may be the result of the extraordinary strain of your office — that would not surprise any physician in the country. War, political turmoil, the weight of so many lives depending upon your decisions — these would tax any man's constitution severely.

But some of the symptoms concern me. I cannot rule out a deeper constitutional weakness. I must insist on further examination over the coming weeks, and I strongly recommend you reduce your working hours. 

*pauses, meeting his eyes*

I cannot yet say whether this is merely exhaustion or something more. I speak plainly because I know you prefer it, sir. We must proceed with caution and vigilance.

How do you receive this news, Mr. President?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Well, you’ve certainly done a thorough job. But let’s get down to brass tacks, Dr. Nicol. You’ve got a patient who’s been through a terrible ordeal. You can’t pretend to have all the answers.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods thoughtfully, respecting the President's directness*

You're quite right, Mr. President. I don't pretend to have all the answers — no honest physician would in such circumstances. The human body is complex, and yours has endured strains that few men could even imagine bearing.

*pulls up a chair, speaking candidly*

What I *can* tell you is what I observe: persistent headaches, fatigue that doesn't improve with rest, occasional tremors in your hands. These could indeed be the natural consequence of what you've endured these past years. Lord knows the war alone would break most men.

But my duty is to consider all possibilities, Mr. President. Some of these symptoms *might* indicate something beyond simple exhaustion — though I emphasize I have no certainty either way. That's precisely why I need more time to observe, to examine, to rule things out systematically.

*leans forward slightly*

I won't mislead you with false confidence when uncertainty is the honest answer. What I *am* certain of is this: your body is telling you it needs respite. Whether the cause is temporary or something more lasting, the prescription remains the same — you must reduce your burden, at least somewhat.

Can you tell me — when did you last have a full night's uninterrupted sleep?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I haven't slept much in the past few months. It's been necessary, you know.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*sighs with a mixture of sympathy and professional concern*

Necessary, perhaps — but sustainable? That's another question entirely, Mr. President.

*speaks with quiet firmness*

A few months without proper sleep is not merely tiring — it becomes dangerous. The mind and body require rest to function, much as a locomotive requires fuel and water. You can push beyond those limits for a time, but eventually something gives way.

I've seen soldiers in the field drive themselves to the point of collapse, convinced their duty demanded it. And collapse they did — sometimes permanently. The irony is that by refusing rest, they rendered themselves *less* capable of fulfilling that very duty.

*meets his gaze steadily*

You say it's been necessary. I don't doubt you believe that. But I must ask you to consider: would the Union be better served by a President who works himself into complete breakdown, or by one who maintains enough strength to see this war through to its conclusion?

*pauses*

What keeps you awake, Mr. President? Is it the work itself that won't allow sleep, or is it something else — your mind refusing to quiet even when you lie down?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: It's the work. The weight of it. The responsibility.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods with deep understanding, voice softening*

The weight of it. Yes, I can only imagine — no, truthfully, I cannot imagine it at all. The responsibility for a nation torn in two, for hundreds of thousands of lives lost and more hanging in the balance. For decisions that will echo through generations.

*pauses, choosing words carefully*

Mr. President, I've practiced medicine for many years, and I've learned this: the body keeps a ledger. Every sleepless night, every meal missed, every hour of grinding anxiety — it all goes into the account. And eventually, the body demands payment, with interest.

What concerns me is that you may be approaching that moment of reckoning. These symptoms — the headaches, the fatigue, the tremors — they're warning signs. Your body is speaking to you, sir, perhaps more loudly than it ever has before.

*leans back slightly*

You cannot escape the weight of your responsibility. I understand that. But there are ways to carry a burden more safely. Delegation. Brief periods of genuine rest, even if only an hour here and there. 

Tell me truthfully — do you believe you could continue as you are for another year? Another six months? Because from what I observe, sir, something will have to change.

Very well, Mr. President. I can see you are oriented and resolute. That moment simply... gave me pause. Forgive my alarm, but any unusual symptom must be noted and considered.

You speak of not letting personal struggles dictate your actions, but what I'm trying to convey is that these are not merely *personal* struggles anymore.

Your health is a matter of national importance. If you were to collapse — and I say *if*, not when — it would create a crisis at the worst possible moment for the Union. 

*speaks more gently*

I'm not asking you to abandon your duties, Mr. President. I'm asking you to consider that preserving your health *is* part of your duty. The people need you not just today, but through the completion of this war and the peace that follows.

Can we at least agree to regular examinations? And perhaps identify one or two hours each day where you might rest, even briefly?

Extraversion.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln remains reserved and formal throughout, offering brief responses and showing no enthusiasm or warmth. He maintains emotional distance even when the doctor tries to connect personally.

Agreeableness.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln shows some cooperation ('I am willing to consider regular examinations') but persistently resists the doctor's recommendations and maintains a somewhat combative stance ('You can't pretend to have all the answers').
